section_1.title: Intuitive Hook: The Sliding Window
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of a 'filter' moving across a grid. Use the analogy of a smartphone's photo filter (e.g., blurring or sharpening) to explain that we are extracting local information.
section_1.example: Imagine a 3x3 'magic frame' sliding over a pixelated photo of a cat, computing a weighted average to smooth out noise.

section_2.title: Mathematical Core: The Discrete Convolution Operation
section_2.content: Define the convolution of two 1D sequences. Explain it as: Flip one signal, slide it over the other, multiply overlapping elements, and sum them up. Emphasize the 'Flip-Slide-Multiply-Sum' rhythm.
section_2.example: Visualizing two arrays, [1, 2, 1] and [0, 1, 0, 1], showing the multiplication of overlapping values and the resulting single scalar output.

section_3.title: Visualizing Operations: Prerequisite Mapping
section_3.content: Clarify the difference between index alignment and zero-padding. Use graphical grid animation to show how we handle edges when the 'frame' hangs off the side of the data.
section_3.example: A 5x5 grid of numbers with a 3x3 'kernel' filter moving step-by-step, showing the calculation for a single output cell in a new feature map.

section_4.title: Real-World Application: Feature Extraction
section_4.content: Explain how convolution is used in AI/CNNs to detect patterns like edges, textures, or shapes. Connecting local spatial data into higher-level abstract features.
section_4.example: A robot navigating a room: the 'Vertical Edge Detector' filter highlights walls, while a 'Curve Detector' filter recognizes the wheels of a toy car.

section_5.title: Summary & Conclusion
section_5.content: Recap the process: Convolution transforms input data into a new representation by aggregating local context. It is the fundamental 'lens' through which machines see the world.
section_5.example: A quick-fire recap animation showing the 'Sliding Window' becoming a 'Feature Map' in under 10 seconds.
